analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act in full and restores the pre-2010 insurance rules.
analysis.headline: A full-repeal bill backed by eight House Republicans was referred to eight committees and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the Affordable Care Act and its companion 2010 law in their entirety, effective October 1, 2018 [S2][S3]. That would end the ban on insurers refusing or charging more for pre-existing conditions, the Medicaid expansion, marketplace subsidies that help people buy coverage, the rule letting young adults stay on a parent's plan, and rules requiring plans to cover essential benefits [S3]. The bill would also roll back the 2010 law that replaced bank-based federal student lending with direct federal loans [S2][S3]. It never reached a floor vote in either chamber [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Insurers, medical device makers, and brand-name drug makers would be freed from Affordable Care Act requirements and taxes. Wealthy households would no longer pay the law's surtax on high incomes and investment gains. Private banks would regain the federal student loan business they lost in 2010.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health industries, private lenders, high earners

how_it_helps.text: Repealing the two 2010 laws restores every provision of law they amended or repealed, as if the laws had never been enacted [S2][S3].
The effective date is October 1, 2018, the start of federal fiscal year 2019 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The tens of millions of people who gained coverage or protections under the law: people with pre-existing conditions, marketplace customers receiving subsidies, newly Medicaid-eligible adults, young adults on their parents' plans, and seniors with lower drug costs. Hospitals and community health providers would also lose the revenue from newly insured patients.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions and subsidized coverage

drawbacks.text: Repeal would restore the pre-2010 insurance market, in which insurers could deny coverage or charge far more based on health status, with no subsidies to help people buy plans [S3].
The bill offers no replacement of any kind; it simply restores the law as it stood before 2010, including the bank-based student loan system the 2010 law had replaced [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gains go to industries and high-income households, while the costs fall on people's health coverage: an estimated tens of millions would lose subsidies, Medicaid expansion coverage, or protections for pre-existing conditions. Unlike the 2017 repeal debates that at least paired repeal with transition plans, this bill contained no replacement provisions at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to eight House committees and to two subcommittees, but no committee ever reported it and the House never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on July 18, 2017, joined by seven Republican cosponsors, all of the House's conservative wing [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to eight full committees at once and then to subcommittees on Health and on Indian, Insular and Alaska Native Affairs in late July 2017 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber [S5].

The bill sat alongside the larger 2017 repeal effort, in which repeal legislation passed the House in 2017 but narrowly failed in the Senate; the House never took up this broader full-repeal version [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on the Affordable Care Act are better off because the bill died: marketplace customers, adults covered by Medicaid expansion, and anyone with a pre-existing condition. Health sectors that grew up around the law's coverage expansion also kept their revenue, while private banks did not get the student loan business back.

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full-repeal bill on July 18, 2017.

for.name: 7 House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only seven cosponsors: Gosar, Garrett, Franks, Gaetz, Hice, Massie, and Gohmert.

against.name: House committees of referral
against.role: Eight committees, including Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote despite full Republican control of the chamber, leaving the repeal effort to the narrower 2017 reconciliation bill instead.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill, and House leadership, also Republican, never brought it to a vote.

industries.note: Repeal would end the marketplace subsidies and the individual requirement that brought insurers millions of subsidized customers, but it would also restore their freedom to deny coverage or price based on health status. The net effect for the public is the loss of guaranteed coverage protections.

industries.industry: Medical device manufacturers and brand-name drug makers
industries.note: Repeal would erase the Affordable Care Act's industry-specific taxes and fees and restore the pre-2010 drug pricing rules. Industry gains come at the cost of the federal revenue and price relief those provisions provided.

The 2010 health law shifted federal student lending from subsidized private banks to direct federal loans; repealing it restores the bank-based system. Borrowers would again route through private middlemen collecting federal subsidies.

Providers would lose the Medicaid expansion payments and insured-patient revenue that came with the law, leaving them with more uncompensated care. Their interest runs alongside patients' interest in keeping coverage.
